source.text: וַיֵּשְׁב֖וּ שָׁלֹ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֑ים אֵ֚ין מִלְחָמָ֔ה בֵּ֥ין אֲרָ֖ם וּבֵ֥ין יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And they remained three years, there was not war between Aram and between Israel.

en.L: And they remained three years; there was no war between Aram and Israel.
en.B: For three years there was no war between Aram and Israel.
en.R: For three years Aram and Israel did not fight each other.

decisions.choice: three years without war: the peace that followed the treaty of 20:34
decisions.reason: Chapter 20 ended with Ahab sparing Ben-hadad king of Aram and making a treaty with him (20:31-34). The three quiet years follow from that treaty; verse 2 dates the new campaign to the third of them.

decisions.choice: Aram: the kingdom of the Arameans, ruled from Damascus
decisions.reason: Aram was the Aramean kingdom north-east of Israel, with Damascus as its capital (20:34). Its king in these chapters is Ben-hadad (20:1).

source.text: וַיְהִ֖י בַּשָּׁנָ֣ה הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֑ית וַיֵּ֛רֶד יְהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֖ה אֶל־מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was in the year the third, and went down Jehoshaphat king of Judah to [the] king of Israel.

en.L: And it happened in the third year that Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to the king of Israel.
en.B: Then in the third year Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to visit Israel's king.
en.R: In the third year, Jehoshaphat king of Judah went to visit the king of Israel.

decisions.choice: 2 Chronicles 18 retells this story
decisions.reason: The account of the campaign against Ramoth-gilead, from Jehoshaphat's visit to Ahab's death (verses 2-35), is told again in 2 Chronicles 18:2-34, in nearly the same words. Chronicles adds that Jehoshaphat had made a marriage alliance with Ahab (2 Chronicles 18:1; compare 2 Kings 8:18) and that a prophet rebuked him afterward for helping Ahab (2 Chronicles 19:1-3).

decisions.choice: the king of Israel: Ahab
decisions.reason: Through most of this story the narrator calls him only "the king of Israel". He is Ahab (16:29; 20:2), and his name appears in verse 20 and again at his death (verses 39-40). Jehoshaphat son of Asa had become king of Judah when Asa died (15:24).

decisions.choice: went down: traveled from Jerusalem north to Samaria
decisions.reason: Jerusalem stands high in the hill country, so a journey away from it is spoken of as going down. Verse 10 shows the kings meeting at Samaria, Ahab's capital.

decisions.choice: went down to visit / went to visit
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "to visit" to make clear this was a royal visit, not an attack. Readable drops "down" (m3).

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אֶל־עֲבָדָ֔יו הַיְדַעְתֶּ֕ם כִּֽי־לָ֖נוּ רָמֹ֣ת גִּלְעָ֑ד וַאֲנַ֣חְנוּ מַחְשִׁ֔ים מִקַּ֣חַת אֹתָ֔הּ מִיַּ֖ד מֶ֥לֶךְ אֲרָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] king of Israel to his servants, do you know that to us [belongs] Ramoth-gilead, and we [are] being inactive from taking it from [the] hand of [the] king of Aram?

en.L: And the king of Israel said to his servants, "Do you know that Ramoth-gilead [belongs] to us, and we are keeping still from taking it from the hand of the king of Aram?"
en.B: The king of Israel said to his officials, "You know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us, yet we are doing nothing to take it back from the king of Aram."
en.R: The king of Israel said to his officials, "You know that the city of Ramoth-gilead belongs to us. But we are doing nothing to take it back from the king of Aram!"

decisions.choice: Ramoth-gilead: an Israelite town east of the Jordan held by Aram
decisions.reason: Ramoth in Gilead lay east of the Jordan, in the territory of Gad. It was one of the cities of refuge (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8) and the seat of one of Solomon's district officers (4:13). In the treaty of 20:34 Ben-hadad promised to return the cities his father had taken from Israel; Ramoth-gilead seems to have stayed in Aram's hands.

decisions.choice: do you know ...?: a question that means "you know"
decisions.reason: The king does not ask for information. He reminds his officials of something they all know, to make his point that it is shameful to do nothing.

decisions.choice: we are keeping still: we are idle, doing nothing
decisions.reason: The verb means to be silent or inactive. The king complains that Israel has made no move to recover the town.

decisions.choice: officials
decisions.reason: The servants of a king are his court officials. Literal keeps "servants"; Balanced and Readable say "officials", as these books do for the king's servants.

decisions.choice: a statement in place of the question
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state as a fact what the Hebrew puts as a question (m2).

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־יְה֣וֹשָׁפָ֔ט הֲתֵלֵ֥ךְ אִתִּ֛י לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה רָמֹ֣ת גִּלְעָ֑ד וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהֽוֹשָׁפָט֙ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כָּמ֧וֹנִי כָמ֛וֹךָ כְּעַמִּ֥י כְעַמֶּ֖ךָ כְּסוּסַ֥י כְּסוּסֶֽיךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said to Jehoshaphat, will you go with me to the battle [at] Ramoth-gilead? And said Jehoshaphat to [the] king of Israel, as me as you, as my people as your people, as my horses as your horses.

en.L: And he said to Jehoshaphat, "Will you go with me to battle at Ramoth-gilead?" And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "As I [am], so [are] you; as my people, so your people; as my horses, so your horses."
en.B: He asked Jehoshaphat, "Will you go with me to fight at Ramoth-gilead?" Jehoshaphat answered the king of Israel, "I am as you are, my troops are as your troops, my horses as your horses."
en.R: Then he turned to Jehoshaphat. "Will you join me in attacking Ramoth-gilead?" he asked. Jehoshaphat told the king of Israel, "I am with you all the way. My army and my horses are yours to command."

decisions.choice: as I am, so are you ...: I am fully with you; all I have is at your disposal
decisions.reason: Jehoshaphat answers with a set saying of alliance. He puts himself, his army and his chariot horses on the same footing as Ahab's, promising to fight alongside him as one force.

decisions.choice: my people as your people: my army as your army
decisions.reason: Here "people" means the fighting men a king leads into battle, as often in these books.

decisions.choice: horses: the horses of the chariot forces
decisions.reason: Horses in Israel and Judah were used above all to draw war chariots (10:26-29). Promising his horses means promising his chariots.

decisions.choice: troops / army
decisions.reason: The army sense of "people" (m2): Literal keeps "people", Balanced says "troops" and Readable "army", as in these books generally.

decisions.choice: I am with you all the way. My army and my horses are yours to command.
decisions.reason: Readable says what the saying means (m1) rather than repeating its pattern three times.

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל דְּרָשׁ־נָ֥א כַיּ֖וֹם אֶת־דְּבַ֥ר יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Jehoshaphat to [the] king of Israel, seek please as the day the word of Yahweh.

en.L: And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Please inquire today for the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."
en.B: But Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "First, please seek the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}."
en.R: But Jehoshaphat also said to the king of Israel, "First, please ask {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says."

decisions.choice: seek the word of Yahweh: ask a prophet for Yahweh's answer before going to war
decisions.reason: Kings asked God before a battle whether to go and whether they would win, usually through a prophet or a priest (1 Samuel 23:2-4; 30:7-8). Jehoshaphat will not set out until this has been done.

decisions.choice: as the day: first, now, before anything else
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean "today" or "at once". Here it asks that the inquiry be made now, before they march.

decisions.choice: First
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "first" for the sense of m2; Literal keeps "today".

source.text: וַיִּקְבֹּ֨ץ מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֥ל אֶֽת־הַנְּבִיאִים֮ כְּאַרְבַּ֣ע מֵא֣וֹת אִישׁ֒ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֗ם הַאֵלֵ֞ךְ עַל־רָמֹ֥ת גִּלְעָ֛ד לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה אִם־אֶחְדָּ֑ל וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ עֲלֵ֔ה וְיִתֵּ֥ן אֲדֹנָ֖י בְּיַ֥ד הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And gathered [the] king of Israel the prophets, about four hundred man, and said to them, shall I go against Ramoth-gilead for battle, or shall I refrain? And they said, go up, and will give the Lord into [the] hand of the king.

en.L: And the king of Israel gathered the prophets, about four hundred men, and said to them, "Shall I go against Ramoth-gilead for battle, or shall I refrain?" And they said, "Go up, and the Lord will give [it] into the hand of the king."
en.B: So the king of Israel gathered the prophets, about four hundred men, and asked them, "Shall I go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I hold back?" "Go up," they said, "for the Lord will give it into the king's hand."
en.R: So the king of Israel called together about four hundred prophets. He asked them, "Should I go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or not?" They answered, "Go! The Lord will help you capture it, Your Majesty."

decisions.choice: the prophets: a large group of court prophets
decisions.reason: These four hundred are prophets attached to Ahab's court. They speak in the name of Yahweh (verses 11-12, 24), unlike the prophets of Baal and Asherah of 18:19, but Jehoshaphat is not satisfied with them (verse 7).

decisions.choice: the Lord: the title "Lord", not the divine name
decisions.reason: In this first answer the prophets say "the Lord" (Adonai), a title, rather than the name Yahweh. In verses 11-12 they use the name. Whether the title here is a sign of vagueness is not clear.

decisions.choice: will give into the hand of the king: an answer that does not name what is given
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has no object: "will give into the hand of the king". The natural sense is that the city will be given to Ahab. The answer is also loose enough to be fulfilled in another way, since it does not say which king or what will be given; verse 15 repeats it, and verses 19-23 show the promise was a deception.

decisions.choice: give into the hand of: give victory over, let capture
decisions.reason: To give something into someone's hand is to put it in their power.

decisions.choice: it
decisions.reason: Balanced supplies "it", the city, as the natural object (m3). Literal brackets the word.

decisions.choice: help you capture it, Your Majesty
decisions.reason: Readable says what "give into the hand" means (m4) and turns "the king" into a direct address, since the prophets are speaking to him.

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יְה֣וֹשָׁפָ֔ט הַאֵ֨ין פֹּ֥ה נָבִ֛יא לַיהוָ֖ה ע֑וֹד וְנִדְרְשָׁ֖ה מֵאוֹתֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Jehoshaphat, is there not here a prophet of Yahweh still, and we may inquire of him?

en.L: And Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not here still a prophet of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, that we may inquire of him?"
en.B: But Jehoshaphat said, "Is there no other prophet of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} here whom we can ask?"
en.R: But Jehoshaphat asked, "Is there not another prophet of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} here? We should ask him too."

decisions.choice: is there not still here a prophet of Yahweh?: is there no other prophet besides these?
decisions.reason: "Still" means "besides" or "in addition". Jehoshaphat does not deny that the four hundred are prophets, but he wants another voice. The question suggests that he does not trust their quick agreement.

decisions.choice: other / another
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable express "still" as "other" (m1).

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל׀אֶֽל־יְהוֹשָׁפָ֡ט ע֣וֹד אִישׁ־אֶחָ֡ד לִדְרֹשׁ֩ אֶת־יְהוָ֨ה מֵאֹת֜וֹ וַאֲנִ֣י שְׂנֵאתִ֗יו כִּ֠י לֹֽא־יִתְנַבֵּ֨א עָלַ֥י טוֹב֙ כִּ֣י אִם־רָ֔ע מִיכָ֖יְהוּ בֶּן־יִמְלָ֑ה וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ יְה֣וֹשָׁפָ֔ט אַל־יֹאמַ֥ר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ כֵּֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] king of Israel to Jehoshaphat, still [there is] one man to inquire of Yahweh from him, and I hate him, for not he prophesies concerning me good but evil, Micaiah son of Imlah. And said Jehoshaphat, not let say the king so.

en.L: And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "[There is] still one man by whom to inquire of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, but I hate him, for he does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil: Micaiah son of Imlah." And Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so."
en.B: The king of Israel answered Jehoshaphat, "There is still one man through whom we could inquire of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him, for his prophecies about me are never good, only bad." Jehoshaphat said, "Let the king not speak like that."
en.R: The king of Israel answered Jehoshaphat, "There is one more man we could ask to find out what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says. But I hate him. He never says anything good about me. He only predicts trouble for me. His name is Micaiah son of Imlah." Jehoshaphat said, "Your Majesty, you should not say that."

decisions.choice: good ... evil: good fortune ... disaster
decisions.reason: "Good" and "evil" here are what the prophecies promise: success or trouble. Ahab complains that Micaiah only ever announces harm for him.

decisions.choice: Micaiah son of Imlah: a prophet of Yahweh known only from this story
decisions.reason: His name means "Who is like Yahweh?" He is not the Micah of the book of Micah, who lived over a century later. Elijah is not mentioned in this chapter.

decisions.choice: let not the king say so: a polite rebuke
decisions.reason: Jehoshaphat speaks of Ahab in the third person, as was polite toward a king. He objects to Ahab's hatred for a prophet of Yahweh, or to the idea that a prophet speaks only to please.

decisions.choice: bad / trouble
decisions.reason: Balanced says "bad" and Readable "trouble" for the sense of "evil" here (m1); Literal keeps "evil".

decisions.choice: Your Majesty, you should not say that
decisions.reason: Readable turns the polite third person (m3) into a direct address.

source.text: וַיִּקְרָא֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶל־סָרִ֖יס אֶחָ֑ד וַיֹּ֕אמֶר מַהֲרָ֖ה מִיכָ֥יְהוּ בֶן־יִמְלָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And called [the] king of Israel to one official, and said, hurry [to bring] Micaiah son of Imlah.

en.L: And the king of Israel called to one official and said, "Hurry [to bring] Micaiah son of Imlah."
en.B: So the king of Israel called one of his court officials and said, "Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once."
en.R: So the king of Israel sent for one of his officials. He told him, "Go and get Micaiah son of Imlah. Hurry!"

decisions.choice: official: a court officer
decisions.reason: The word can mean a eunuch, but it is also the ordinary word for a high officer at a royal court, which is the sense here; nothing in the story turns on whether he was a eunuch.

decisions.choice: hurry Micaiah: bring Micaiah quickly
decisions.reason: The verb "hurry" takes Micaiah as its object: "make Micaiah come quickly".

decisions.choice: official
decisions.reason: Every level says "official" (m1). Literal may say "eunuch" where that sense matters; here it does not.

source.text: וּמֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֡ל וִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֡ה יֹשְׁבִים֩ אִ֨ישׁ עַל־כִּסְא֜וֹ מְלֻבָּשִׁ֤ים בְּגָדִים֙ בְּגֹ֔רֶן פֶּ֖תַח שַׁ֣עַר שֹׁמְר֑וֹן וְכָ֨ל־הַנְּבִיאִ֔ים מִֽתְנַבְּאִ֖ים לִפְנֵיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah [were] sitting each on his throne, clothed [in] garments, at [the] threshing floor [at the] entrance of [the] gate of Samaria; and all the prophets [were] prophesying before them.

en.L: And the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah [were] sitting each on his throne, clothed in robes, at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria; and all the prophets [were] prophesying before them.
en.B: Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, dressed in their royal robes, at the threshing floor at the entrance to the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying in front of them.
en.R: The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah sat on their thrones in their royal robes. They were at the threshing floor by the entrance to the city gate of Samaria. All the prophets were there in front of them, prophesying.

decisions.choice: clothed in garments: wearing royal robes
decisions.reason: "Garments" here are the formal robes of kings seated in state. The scene is a public royal assembly.

decisions.choice: the threshing floor at the gate of Samaria: a broad open space outside the city gate
decisions.reason: A threshing floor was a flat, open area of hard ground. One by the city gate made room for the two kings' thrones and the crowd of four hundred prophets. The gate was the place for public business and judgment.

decisions.choice: prophesying: speaking as prophets, perhaps with ecstatic behavior
decisions.reason: The verb form can describe a prophet's words or the excited behavior that sometimes went with prophecy (1 Samuel 10:5-6; 18:29 in this book). Here the next verses show both actions and words.

decisions.choice: royal robes
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "royal" to show what kind of robes these were (m1).

source.text: וַיַּ֥עַשׂ ל֛וֹ צִדְקִיָּ֥ה בֶֽן־כְּנַעֲנָ֖ה קַרְנֵ֣י בַרְזֶ֑ל וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ כֹּֽה־אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה בְּאֵ֛לֶּה תְּנַגַּ֥ח אֶת־אֲרָ֖ם עַד־כַּלֹּתָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And made for himself Zedekiah son of Chenaanah horns of iron, and said, thus says Yahweh, with these you will gore Aram until finishing them.

en.L: And Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: 'With these you will gore Aram until they are finished.'"
en.B: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made himself iron horns, and he said, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: 'With these you will gore the Arameans until they are destroyed.'"
en.R: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made some horns out of iron. He said, "This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: 'With horns like these you will gore the Arameans and wipe them out.'"

decisions.choice: horns of iron: a sign acted out by the prophet
decisions.reason: Prophets sometimes acted out their message (11:29-31; 2 Kings 13:15-19). The horn of a bull stands for strength and conquest (Deuteronomy 33:17). With iron horns Zedekiah pictures the king as a bull goring Aram to death.

decisions.choice: made: had made, before the scene
decisions.reason: The horns were most likely made before the assembly at the gate, and Zedekiah now shows them; the verb does not require that he made them on the spot.

decisions.choice: Aram: the Aramean people and army
decisions.reason: The country's name stands for its people and army, as the plural "them" at the end shows.

decisions.choice: The LORD says this / This is what the LORD says
decisions.reason: The messenger formula "thus says Yahweh" has one wording at each level in these books. Balanced and Readable name the Arameans (m3).

source.text: וְכָל־הַנְּבִאִ֔ים נִבְּאִ֥ים כֵּ֖ן לֵאמֹ֑ר עֲלֵ֞ה רָמֹ֤ת גִּלְעָד֙ וְהַצְלַ֔ח וְנָתַ֥ן יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַ֥ד הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And all the prophets [were] prophesying so, saying, go up [to] Ramoth-gilead and succeed, and will give Yahweh [it] into [the] hand of the king.

en.L: And all the prophets [were] prophesying so, saying, "Go up [to] Ramoth-gilead and succeed, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will give [it] into the hand of the king."
en.B: All the prophets were prophesying the same thing: "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and be victorious. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will give it into the king's hand."
en.R: All the other prophets were saying the same thing: "Attack Ramoth-gilead and win the battle! {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will help you capture it, Your Majesty."

decisions.choice: succeed: prosper, win
decisions.reason: The verb means to succeed or prosper; in a battle it means victory. Micaiah repeats the words mockingly in verse 15.

decisions.choice: will give into the hand of the king: as in verse 6, now with the divine name
decisions.reason: This time the prophets use the name Yahweh. As in verse 6 the Hebrew leaves the object unstated.

decisions.choice: help you capture it, Your Majesty
decisions.reason: As in verse 6.

source.text: וְהַמַּלְאָ֞ךְ אֲשֶׁר־הָלַ֣ךְ׀לִקְרֹ֣א מִיכָ֗יְהוּ דִּבֶּ֤ר אֵלָיו֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר הִנֵּה־נָ֞א דִּבְרֵ֧י הַנְּבִיאִ֛ים פֶּֽה־אֶחָ֥ד ט֖וֹב אֶל־הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ יְהִֽי־נָ֣א דְבָרְךָ֗ כִּדְבַ֛ר אַחַ֥ד מֵהֶ֖ם וְדִבַּ֥רְתָּ טּֽוֹב׃

records.literal_gloss: And the messenger who had gone to call Micaiah spoke to him, saying, look please, [the] words of the prophets [are with] one mouth good to the king; let be please your word like [the] word of one of them, and you will speak good.

en.L: And the messenger who had gone to call Micaiah spoke to him, saying, "Look, please, the words of the prophets [are] one mouth, good to the king. Let your word, please, be like the word of one of them, and speak good."
en.B: The messenger who had gone to call Micaiah said to him, "Listen, the prophets are all speaking with one voice, and what they say is good for the king. Please let your word be like one of theirs, and speak favorably."
en.R: The messenger who went to get Micaiah said to him, "Listen! All the other prophets agree. They are all promising the king success. Please say the same thing they are saying. Give him a good message."

decisions.choice: one mouth: with one voice, in full agreement
decisions.reason: "One mouth" means that the prophets all say the same thing.

decisions.choice: good: favorable, promising success
decisions.reason: As in verse 8, "good" is a message of success for the king. The messenger presses Micaiah to agree with the others.

decisions.choice: speaking with one voice / all agree
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the English idiom closest to "one mouth"; Readable says what it means (m1).

source.text: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר מִיכָ֑יְהוּ חַי־יְהוָ֕ה כִּ֠י אֶת־אֲשֶׁ֨ר יֹאמַ֧ר יְהוָ֛ה אֵלַ֖י אֹת֥וֹ אֲדַבֵּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Micaiah, [by the] life of Yahweh, that what will say Yahweh to me, it I will speak.

en.L: And Micaiah said, "[As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says to me, that I will speak."
en.B: But Micaiah said, "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, whatever {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says to me is what I will speak."
en.R: But Micaiah said, "I promise, as surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, I will say only what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} tells me to say."

decisions.choice: as Yahweh lives: an oath
decisions.reason: Micaiah binds himself by an oath in Yahweh's name, the strongest form of promise. He will not shape his message to please the king.

decisions.choice: what Yahweh says to me, that I will speak: the mark of a true prophet
decisions.reason: A prophet of Yahweh speaks only the words Yahweh gives him (Numbers 22:38; Deuteronomy 18:18). Micaiah's oath sets him apart from prophets who say what the king wants to hear.

decisions.choice: I promise
decisions.reason: Readable adds "I promise" to show that "as surely as the LORD lives" is an oath (m1).

source.text: וַיָּבוֹא֮ אֶל־הַמֶּלֶךְ֒ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ אֵלָ֗יו מִיכָ֨יְהוּ֙ הֲנֵלֵ֞ךְ אֶל־רָמֹ֥ת גִּלְעָ֛ד לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה אִם־נֶחְדָּ֑ל וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ עֲלֵ֣ה וְהַצְלַ֔ח וְנָתַ֥ן יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַ֥ד הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he came to the king, and said the king to him, Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead for battle, or shall we refrain? And he said to him, go up and succeed, and will give Yahweh [it] into [the] hand of the king.

en.L: And he came to the king, and the king said to him, "Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead for battle, or shall we refrain?" And he said to him, "Go up and succeed, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will give [it] into the hand of the king."
en.B: When he came to the king, the king asked him, "Micaiah, shall we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall we hold back?" He answered, "Go up and be victorious. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will give it into the king's hand."
en.R: When Micaiah came, the king said, "Micaiah, should we march on Ramoth-gilead, or not?" Micaiah answered, "Attack and win the battle! {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} will help you capture it, Your Majesty."

decisions.choice: go up and succeed: the other prophets' words repeated, not Micaiah's real message
decisions.reason: Micaiah answers with the exact words of the four hundred (verse 12). The king's reply in verse 16 shows that he heard them as mockery, or at least knew they were not what Micaiah had received from Yahweh. Micaiah gives his true message in verse 17.

decisions.choice: shall we go: the king now includes Jehoshaphat
decisions.reason: In verse 6 the king asked "shall I go"; now, in front of Jehoshaphat, he says "we".

decisions.choice: help you capture it, Your Majesty
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the same wording as in verse 12, so the reader can see that Micaiah repeats the prophets.

source.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ עַד־כַּמֶּ֥ה פְעָמִ֖ים אֲנִ֣י מַשְׁבִּעֶ֑ךָ אֲ֠שֶׁר לֹֽא־תְדַבֵּ֥ר אֵלַ֛י רַק־אֱמֶ֖ת בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said to him the king, until how many times [am] I making you swear that not you will speak to me only truth in [the] name of Yahweh?

en.L: And the king said to him, "How many times must I make you swear that you will speak to me nothing but truth in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"
en.B: But the king said to him, "How often must I put you under oath to tell me only the truth in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}?"
en.R: But the king said to him, "How often must I say this? Swear in the name of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that you will tell me only the truth!"

decisions.choice: how many times must I make you swear?: an angry demand, not a real question
decisions.reason: The king is not counting. He is irritated that Micaiah is not giving him Yahweh's real answer, which suggests he knows the earlier answer was not it, and he puts him under oath.

decisions.choice: in the name of Yahweh: speaking as Yahweh's spokesman
decisions.reason: To speak in Yahweh's name is to speak with his authority, as his messenger (Deuteronomy 18:20-22).

decisions.choice: How many times do I have to tell you? Swear ...
decisions.reason: Readable splits the angry question into a question and a command, keeping its force.

source.text: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר רָאִ֤יתִי אֶת־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ נְפֹצִ֣ים אֶל־הֶהָרִ֔ים כַּצֹּ֕אן אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֵין־לָהֶ֖ם רֹעֶ֑ה וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ לֹֽא־אֲדֹנִ֣ים לָאֵ֔לֶּה יָשׁ֥וּבוּ אִישׁ־לְבֵית֖וֹ בְּשָׁלֽוֹם׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains like the flock which there is not to them a shepherd; and said Yahweh, not masters to these; let them return each to his house in peace.

en.L: And he said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, \q like sheep that have no shepherd. \q And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'These have no master; \q let them return each to his house in peace.'"
en.B: Then Micaiah said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the hills, \q like sheep that have no shepherd. \q And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'These have no master; \q let each of them go home in peace.'"
en.R: Then Micaiah said, "I saw the whole army of Israel scattered over the hills, \q like sheep without anyone to shepherd them. \q And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'These men have no master now. \q Let each of them go home in peace.'"

decisions.choice: like sheep that have no shepherd: a people whose king is gone
decisions.reason: A king was the shepherd of his people. Moses asked Yahweh for a leader so that his people would not be "like sheep that have no shepherd" (Numbers 27:17). Micaiah sees Israel's army scattered after the battle, leaderless: the king will die.

decisions.choice: these have no master; let them return in peace: the soldiers go home unharmed, without their king
decisions.reason: "Master" (literally "masters", a plural used for one lord) here is the king. The army will not be destroyed; it will go home, but without him (verse 36).

decisions.choice: a vision set as a short poem
decisions.reason: Micaiah reports what he saw and heard in two balanced pairs of lines, the form prophets often used for their messages.

decisions.choice: all Israel: Israel's army in the field
decisions.reason: The scattered flock is the army Ahab leads to Ramoth-gilead.

decisions.choice: the whole army of Israel / These men ... now
decisions.reason: Readable makes explicit that the vision is of the army (m4) and that "no master" refers to what will happen after the battle (m2).

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֶל־יְהוֹשָׁפָ֑ט הֲלוֹא֙ אָמַ֣רְתִּי אֵלֶ֔יךָ לֽוֹא־יִתְנַבֵּ֥א עָלַ֛י ט֖וֹב כִּ֥י אִם־רָֽע׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] king of Israel to Jehoshaphat, did not I say to you, not he prophesies concerning me good but evil?

en.L: And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not say to you, 'He does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil'?"
en.B: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not say to you that he prophesies nothing good about me, only bad?"
en.R: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I told you so! He never says anything good about me. He only predicts trouble."

decisions.choice: did I not say to you?: "I told you"
decisions.reason: The question expects agreement. The king turns Micaiah's warning into proof of personal hostility (verse 8) instead of hearing it as Yahweh's word.

decisions.choice: I told you so!
decisions.reason: Readable states as a fact what the king asks as a question (m1). "Bad" and "trouble" as in verse 8.

source.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לָכֵ֖ן שְׁמַ֣ע דְּבַר־יְהוָ֑ה רָאִ֤יתִי אֶת־יְהוָה֙ יֹשֵׁ֣ב עַל־כִּסְא֔וֹ וְכָל־צְבָ֤א הַשָּׁמַ֨יִם֙ עֹמֵ֣ד עָלָ֔יו מִימִינ֖וֹ וּמִשְּׂמֹאלֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, therefore hear [the] word of Yahweh: I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne, and all [the] host of the heavens standing by him, from his right and from his left.

en.L: And he said, "Therefore hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: I saw {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sitting on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right and on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.
en.B: Micaiah went on, "Then hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. I saw {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} seated on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} throne, with all the host of heaven standing around {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right and on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.
en.R: Micaiah said, "Then listen to what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says. I saw {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sitting on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} throne. All the armies of heaven were standing around {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right side and on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.

decisions.choice: I saw Yahweh on his throne: a vision of Yahweh's heavenly court
decisions.reason: Micaiah tells of a vision in which he saw Yahweh as a king holding court, surrounded by his attendants. Isaiah saw Yahweh on his throne in a similar way (Isaiah 6:1-8), and Job 1:6 and 2:1 describe heavenly beings presenting themselves before Yahweh. Micaiah claims to have stood in that council (compare Jeremiah 23:18, 22), unlike the other prophets.

decisions.choice: the host of heaven: the heavenly beings who serve Yahweh
decisions.reason: "Host" means an army. Here the host of heaven is Yahweh's company of heavenly attendants, gathered around his throne like the officials of a royal court. Elsewhere the same phrase can mean the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19).

decisions.choice: therefore: because you will not listen, hear what I saw
decisions.reason: Micaiah answers the king's charge of hostility (verse 18) by explaining where his message came from.

decisions.choice: all the armies of heaven
decisions.reason: Readable says "armies" for "host", the same word used in the title "the LORD of Armies" in these books (m2).

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֗ה מִ֤י יְפַתֶּה֙ אֶת־אַחְאָ֔ב וְיַ֕עַל וְיִפֹּ֖ל בְּרָמֹ֣ת גִּלְעָ֑ד וַיֹּ֤אמֶר זֶה֙ בְּכֹ֔ה וְזֶ֥ה אֹמֵ֖ר בְּכֹֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Yahweh, who will entice Ahab, and he will go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead? And said this [one] thus, and this [one was] saying thus.

en.L: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'Who will entice Ahab, so that he goes up and falls at Ramoth-gilead?' And one said one thing, and another was saying another.
en.B: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'Who will entice Ahab to go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' Some suggested one thing and some another.
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} asked, 'Who will trick Ahab into attacking Ramoth-gilead, so that he will die there?' One of them suggested one thing, and another suggested something else.

decisions.choice: entice: lure, persuade by deceiving
decisions.reason: The verb means to persuade someone, often by deception, to do what will harm him (Judges 14:15; 16:5; Jeremiah 20:7). It is used again in verses 21-22.

decisions.choice: fall: die in battle
decisions.reason: To fall at a place is to be killed there in battle.

decisions.choice: Ahab: the king of Israel is named
decisions.reason: This is the first time in the chapter that the king of Israel is named. In Yahweh's council the king is called by his name, Ahab.

decisions.choice: trick ... into attacking ... so that he will die there
decisions.reason: Readable says "trick" for "entice" (m1) and says plainly what "go up and fall" means (m2).

source.text: וַיֵּצֵ֣א הָר֗וּחַ וַֽיַּעֲמֹד֙ לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אֲנִ֣י אֲפַתֶּ֑נּוּוַיֹּ֧אמֶר יְהוָ֛ה אֵלָ֖יו בַּמָּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And came out the spirit and stood before Yahweh, and said, I will entice him. And said Yahweh to him, by what?

en.L: And the spirit came out and stood before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, 'I will entice him.' And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, 'By what [means]?'
en.B: Then a spirit came forward and stood before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, 'I will entice him.' {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} asked him, 'How?'
en.R: Then a spirit came forward and stood in front of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. The spirit said, 'I will trick him.' {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} asked, 'How will you do it?'

decisions.choice: verse numbers: Hebrew 22:21 ends with the LORD's question
decisions.reason: This translation numbers verses as the Hebrew text does. In the Hebrew text verse 21 ends with Yahweh's question, "By what?" Many Bibles print that question at the start of verse 22. From verse 44 on, the numbering differs again (see there). The words are the same; only the numbers differ.

decisions.choice: the spirit: one of the heavenly beings in Yahweh's court
alternatives: a spirit known for this task
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "the spirit", with "the". It may mean simply the particular spirit who stepped forward from the host of verse 19, or a spirit known for this work, or the spirit that moves prophets to speak (compare verse 24). It is not identified further. Spirits sent by God on a task of judgment appear also in Judges 9:23 and 1 Samuel 16:14.

decisions.choice: a spirit
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "a spirit": in English "the spirit" here would suggest a spirit already mentioned or the Spirit of God, and none has been named. Literal keeps the Hebrew "the" (m2).

source.text: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אֵצֵא֙ וְהָיִ֨יתִי֙ ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר בְּפִ֖י כָּל־נְבִיאָ֑יו וַיֹּ֗אמֶר תְּפַתֶּה֙ וְגַם־תּוּכָ֔ל צֵ֖א וַעֲשֵׂה־כֵֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: And he said, I will go out and I will be a spirit of falsehood in [the] mouth of all his prophets. And he said, you will entice and also you will prevail; go out and do so.

en.L: And he said, 'I will go out, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, 'You will entice [him], and you will also succeed; go out and do so.'
en.B: He said, 'I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'You will entice him, and you will succeed. Go and do it.'
en.R: The spirit said, 'I will go out and make all of Ahab's prophets tell lies.' {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said, 'You will trick him, and you will succeed. Go and do it.'

decisions.choice: a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets: Yahweh lets a spirit deceive Ahab's prophets, as judgment on Ahab
alternatives: Yahweh actively sends the deceiving spirit
Yahweh permits a deception Ahab has chosen
the council scene is a vision-picture of Yahweh's judgment
decisions.reason: In Micaiah's vision Yahweh himself asks who will lure Ahab to his death, and he sends the spirit who offers to make Ahab's prophets lie. The passage presents this as Yahweh's judgment on Ahab, already announced for his murder of Naboth (21:19-24). Ahab had long preferred prophets who told him what he wanted to hear (verse 8), and the deception confirms the choice he had made. Yet by telling Ahab the whole vision, Yahweh, through Micaiah, warns him plainly and leaves him free to stay home (verses 23, 28). Scripture elsewhere says that God does not lie (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29), and it speaks of God sending deception on those who refuse the truth (Ezekiel 14:9; 2 Thessalonians 2:11). Whether Micaiah's account is a literal report of a heavenly scene or a vision cast in the picture of a royal council is not stated.

decisions.choice: a spirit of falsehood: a lying spirit
decisions.reason: "Falsehood" describes what the spirit produces: the prophets' words will be false. The phrase is repeated in verse 23.

decisions.choice: you will entice and also prevail: Yahweh's permission and promise of success
decisions.reason: Yahweh's reply grants the spirit's proposal and declares it will work, then sends it out.

decisions.choice: [him] / him
decisions.reason: English needs an object for "entice"; Literal brackets it.

decisions.choice: make all of Ahab's prophets tell lies
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "a lying spirit in the mouth of" the prophets means.

source.text: וְעַתָּ֗ה הִנֵּ֨ה נָתַ֤ן יְהוָה֙ ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר בְּפִ֖י כָּל־נְבִיאֶ֣יךָ אֵ֑לֶּה וַֽיהוָ֔ה דִּבֶּ֥ר עָלֶ֖יךָ רָעָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And now, look, has put Yahweh a spirit of falsehood in [the] mouth of all your prophets these, and Yahweh has spoken concerning you evil.

en.L: And now, look, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has spoken evil concerning you."
en.B: So now, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these prophets of yours. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has decreed disaster for you."
en.R: So you see, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has made all these prophets of yours tell lies. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has decided that disaster will come to you."

decisions.choice: Yahweh has put a lying spirit in their mouths: the vision applied to Ahab
decisions.reason: Micaiah draws the conclusion of the vision: the unanimous voice of the four hundred is not evidence of truth but the very deception Yahweh allowed (see verse 22). In telling Ahab this, Micaiah gives him the truth the other prophets withheld.

decisions.choice: spoken evil concerning you: announced disaster for you
decisions.reason: "Evil" here, as in verses 8 and 18, is harm or calamity, not wrongdoing. When Yahweh speaks it, it is decreed.

decisions.choice: decreed / decided
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable express that Yahweh's spoken word settles what will happen (m2).

source.text: וַיִּגַּשׁ֙ צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ בֶֽן־כְּנַעֲנָ֔ה וַיַּכֶּ֥ה אֶת־מִיכָ֖יְהוּ עַל־הַלֶּ֑חִי וַיֹּ֕אמֶר אֵי־זֶ֨ה עָבַ֧ר רֽוּחַ־יְהוָ֛ה מֵאִתִּ֖י לְדַבֵּ֥ר אוֹתָֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And came near Zedekiah son of Chenaanah and struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said, where [is] this [way that] passed [the] Spirit of Yahweh from with me to speak with you?

en.L: And Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "Which way did the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} pass from me to speak with you?"
en.B: Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came up and slapped Micaiah on the cheek. "Which way did the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} take from me to speak to you?" he asked.
en.R: Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah walked up to Micaiah and slapped him across the face. He said, "Do you really think the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} left me and went to speak to you?"

decisions.choice: struck on the cheek: a public insult
decisions.reason: A slap on the cheek was an act of contempt and humiliation more than an attack to injure (Job 16:10; Lamentations 3:30; Micah 5:1).

decisions.choice: which way did the Spirit pass from me?: a mocking question
decisions.reason: Zedekiah claims that Yahweh's Spirit spoke through him, and scorns the idea that the Spirit could have left him to give Micaiah a different message. His words also echo Micaiah's vision, in which a spirit went out to speak through the prophets (verses 21-23).

decisions.choice: the Spirit of Yahweh: the power by which a prophet speaks
decisions.reason: Prophets spoke when Yahweh's Spirit came on them (Numbers 11:25-29; 1 Samuel 10:6, 10). Zedekiah claims this Spirit; Micaiah's vision has just told the king that a lying spirit was at work in these prophets.

decisions.choice: Do you really think ...?
decisions.reason: Readable brings out the scorn of the question (m2) instead of the "which way" pattern, which is hard to follow in plain English.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מִיכָ֔יְהוּ הִנְּךָ֥ רֹאֶ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא אֲשֶׁ֥ר תָּבֹ֛א חֶ֥דֶר בְּחֶ֖דֶר לְהֵחָבֵֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Micaiah, look, you [are] seeing on that day when you go [into a] room within [a] room to hide yourself.

en.L: And Micaiah said, "Look, you will see on that day when you go into an inner room to hide yourself."
en.B: Micaiah replied, "You will find out on the day you go into an inner room to hide."
en.R: Micaiah answered, "You will find out on the day you run into a back room to hide."

decisions.choice: a room within a room: an inner room
decisions.reason: The phrase means a room deep inside a house, where someone could hide (20:30).

decisions.choice: you will see: you will find out who spoke truly
decisions.reason: Micaiah answers Zedekiah's question by pointing to the day his prophecy is proved false and he has to hide for his life, perhaps when the defeat is known or when the king's successor deals with the prophets who misled him. The text does not tell what happened to Zedekiah.

decisions.choice: find out
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "find out" for "see", the sense here (m2).

source.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל קַ֚ח אֶת־מִיכָ֔יְהוּ וַהֲשִׁיבֵ֖הוּ אֶל־אָמֹ֣ן שַׂר־הָעִ֑יר וְאֶל־יוֹאָ֖שׁ בֶּן־הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] king of Israel, take Micaiah and return him to Amon [the] governor of the city and to Joash son of the king,

en.L: And the king of Israel said, "Take Micaiah and return him to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son,
en.B: Then the king of Israel ordered, "Take Micaiah and send him back to Amon, the city governor, and to Joash, the king's son,
en.R: Then the king of Israel said, "Arrest Micaiah! Take him back to Amon, who governs the city, and to Joash, the king's son.

decisions.choice: return him: send him back to those who had kept him
decisions.reason: "Return" suggests that Micaiah had been in the keeping of these officials before he was called, perhaps already under arrest.

decisions.choice: the official of the city: the governor of Samaria
decisions.reason: The word for an official or commander, with "of the city", names the officer in charge of the capital (2 Kings 23:8).

decisions.choice: the king's son: a royal son, or a title of a royal officer
decisions.reason: Joash may have been one of Ahab's sons. "The king's son" may also be the title of an officer who guarded prisoners (Jeremiah 36:26; 38:6).

decisions.choice: governor
decisions.reason: Every level says "governor", the clearest English for the officer in charge of a city (m2), rather than "prince" or "official".

source.text: וְאָמַרְתָּ֗ כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ שִׂ֥ימוּ אֶת־זֶ֖ה בֵּ֣ית הַכֶּ֑לֶא וְהַאֲכִילֻ֨הוּ לֶ֤חֶם לַ֨חַץ֙ וּמַ֣יִם לַ֔חַץ עַ֖ד בֹּאִ֥י בְשָׁלֽוֹם׃

records.literal_gloss: and you shall say, thus says the king, put this [one in the] house of the prison, and feed him bread of oppression and water of oppression until I come in peace.

en.L: and say, 'Thus says the king: "Put this [man] in the prison house, and feed him bread of affliction and water of affliction until I come in peace."'"
en.B: and tell them, 'The king says this: "Put this man in prison and feed him with scant bread and scant water until I come back safely."'"
en.R: Tell them the king says to put this man in prison. Give him only a little bread and water until I come back safely."

decisions.choice: bread of oppression and water of oppression: the meager rations of a prisoner
decisions.reason: "Oppression" describes hardship. The phrase means bare, reduced rations of bread and water (compare Isaiah 30:20).

decisions.choice: until I come in peace: until I return safely
decisions.reason: The king assumes he will come back unharmed, which is exactly what Micaiah has denied. Micaiah takes up the words in verse 28.

decisions.choice: scant bread and scant water
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the two parallel phrases while saying what they mean (m1).

decisions.choice: indirect speech
decisions.reason: Readable turns the message inside the order into indirect speech, to avoid quotation marks three deep.

source.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מִיכָ֔יְהוּ אִם־שׁ֤וֹב תָּשׁוּב֙ בְּשָׁל֔וֹם לֹֽא־דִבֶּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה בִּ֑י וַיֹּ֕אמֶר שִׁמְע֖וּ עַמִּ֥ים כֻּלָּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Micaiah, if returning you return in peace, not has spoken Yahweh by me. And he said, hear, peoples, all of them.

en.L: And Micaiah said, "If you indeed return in peace, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has not spoken by me." And he said, "Hear, peoples, all of them."
en.B: Micaiah said, "If you ever come back safely, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has not spoken through me." And he added, "Listen, all you peoples!"
en.R: Micaiah said, "If you ever come back safely, then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has not spoken through me." Then he said to everyone there, "Remember what I have said!"

decisions.choice: if you return in peace, Yahweh has not spoken by me: the test of a prophet
decisions.reason: The law gave this test: a prophecy that does not come true was not spoken by Yahweh (Deuteronomy 18:21-22). Micaiah stakes his standing as a prophet on the king's death.

decisions.choice: hear, peoples, all of them: the opening words of the book of Micah
decisions.reason: The same words begin the prophecy of Micah (Micah 1:2). Here they call everyone present to witness what Micaiah has said. The phrase is missing from the main ancient Greek translation of Kings, and some think it was added by a copier who linked Micaiah with the later prophet Micah; it is in the Hebrew text and in 2 Chronicles 18:27.

decisions.choice: peoples: everyone present, or the nations
decisions.reason: "Peoples" usually means nations. Here it is a call to all who hear, to bear witness.

decisions.choice: he said to everyone there, "Remember what I have said!"
decisions.reason: Readable says what the call is for (m2, m3): those present are to witness the prophecy.

source.text: וַיַּ֧עַל מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל וְיהוֹשָׁפָ֥טמֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֖ה רָמֹ֥ת גִּלְעָֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And went up [the] king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah [to] Ramoth-gilead.

en.L: And the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up [to] Ramoth-gilead.
en.B: So the king of Israel went up to Ramoth-gilead, and Jehoshaphat king of Judah with him.
en.R: So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went to attack Ramoth-gilead.

decisions.choice: went up: marched to battle
decisions.reason: "Go up" was the word of the prophets' promise (verses 6, 12, 15) and of Yahweh's question (verse 20). The king does what the deception was meant to make him do.

decisions.choice: went to attack
decisions.reason: Readable says what "went up" means here (m1).

source.text: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ מֶ֨לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל אֶל־יְהוֹשָׁפָ֗ט הִתְחַפֵּשׂ֙ וָבֹ֣א בַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וְאַתָּ֖ה לְבַ֣שׁ בְּגָדֶ֑יךָ וַיִּתְחַפֵּשׂ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיָּב֖וֹא בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And said [the] king of Israel to Jehoshaphat, disguising myself and going into the battle, and you, wear your garments. And disguised himself [the] king of Israel and went into the battle.

en.L: And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "[I will] disguise myself and go into the battle, but you, put on your robes." And the king of Israel disguised himself and went into the battle.
en.B: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will go into the battle in disguise, but you should put on your royal robes." So the king of Israel disguised himself and went into the fight.
en.R: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will dress like an ordinary soldier when I go into battle, but you should wear your royal robes." So the king of Israel put on a disguise and went to fight.

decisions.choice: disguising myself and going: an infinitive used as a statement of intention
decisions.reason: The Hebrew uses two infinitives, a short, clipped way of saying "I will disguise myself and go".

decisions.choice: the king's disguise: an attempt to escape the prophecy
decisions.reason: Ahab tries to make himself unrecognizable so that he cannot be singled out, perhaps having heard of the Aramean order (verse 31) or fearing Micaiah's word. Jehoshaphat, in royal robes, becomes the obvious target (verse 32). Saul too disguised himself before his final battle (1 Samuel 28:8), and Josiah would later do the same (2 Chronicles 35:22).

decisions.choice: dress like an ordinary soldier
decisions.reason: Readable says what the disguise was for, the first time; it then uses "disguised".

source.text: וּמֶ֣לֶךְ אֲרָ֡ם צִוָּ֣ה אֶת־שָׂרֵי֩ הָרֶ֨כֶב אֲשֶׁר־ל֜וֹ שְׁלֹשִׁ֤ים וּשְׁנַ֨יִם֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר לֹ֚א תִּלָּ֣חֲמ֔וּ אֶת־קָטֹ֖ן וְאֶת־גָּד֑וֹל כִּ֛י אִֽם־אֶת־מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְבַדּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] king of Aram had commanded [the] commanders of the chariotry that [were] his, thirty and two, saying, not you shall fight with small and with great, but with [the] king of Israel by himself.

en.L: And the king of Aram had commanded the commanders of the chariots that [were] his, thirty-two, saying, "Do not fight with small or with great, but with the king of Israel alone."
en.B: Now the king of Aram had given an order to his thirty-two chariot commanders: "Fight with no one, small or great, but the king of Israel alone."
en.R: The king of Aram had given orders to his thirty-two chariot commanders: "Do not attack anyone except the king of Israel."

decisions.choice: small and great: anyone at all
decisions.reason: Naming the two extremes means everyone. The Aramean chariots are to ignore every other soldier and hunt down the king.

decisions.choice: thirty-two commanders: the officers who replaced the thirty-two kings
decisions.reason: Ben-hadad had once led thirty-two allied kings (20:1, 16); after his defeat he was advised to replace them with commanders (20:24). These are presumably the same thirty-two posts.

decisions.choice: the king of Israel alone: the target is the king
decisions.reason: Killing the enemy king would end the battle. The order explains Ahab's disguise and the danger to Jehoshaphat in his royal robes.

decisions.choice: anyone
decisions.reason: Readable drops the pair "small or great" and says "anyone" (m1).

source.text: וַיְהִ֡י כִּרְאוֹת֩ שָׂרֵ֨י הָרֶ֜כֶב אֶת־יְהוֹשָׁפָ֗ט וְהֵ֤מָּה אָֽמְרוּ֙ אַ֣ךְ מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל ה֔וּא וַיָּסֻ֥רוּ עָלָ֖יו לְהִלָּחֵ֑ם וַיִּזְעַ֖ק יְהוֹשָׁפָֽט׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, when saw [the] commanders of the chariotry Jehoshaphat, and they said, surely [the] king of Israel [is] he; and they turned against him to fight, and cried out Jehoshaphat.

en.L: And it happened, when the commanders of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, that they said, "Surely he [is] the king of Israel." And they turned aside against him to fight, and Jehoshaphat cried out.
en.B: When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "Surely that is the king of Israel!" So they turned to attack him, and Jehoshaphat cried out.
en.R: When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat in his royal robes, they said, "That must be the king of Israel!" So they turned to attack him. But Jehoshaphat shouted out.

decisions.choice: Jehoshaphat cried out: a cry for help, or a shout that showed who he was
decisions.reason: The verb is used for crying out in distress, often to God. 2 Chronicles 18:31 adds "and Yahweh helped him, and God drew them away from him". In Kings the cry may simply have revealed that he was not Ahab, perhaps by a battle cry of Judah or by his voice.

decisions.choice: surely: "it must be"
decisions.reason: The commanders draw the natural conclusion from the royal robes.

decisions.choice: in his royal robes
decisions.reason: Readable reminds the reader why they took him for the king (verse 30).

source.text: וַיְהִ֗י כִּרְאוֹת֙ שָׂרֵ֣י הָרֶ֔כֶב כִּֽי־לֹא־מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל ה֑וּא וַיָּשׁ֖וּבוּ מֵאַחֲרָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And it was, when saw [the] commanders of the chariotry that not [the] king of Israel [was] he, and they turned back from after him.

en.L: And it happened, when the commanders of the chariots saw that he [was] not the king of Israel, that they turned back from pursuing him.
en.B: Once the chariot commanders saw he was not Israel's king, they broke off the chase.
en.R: When the chariot commanders realized he was not the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him.

decisions.choice: turned back from after him: stopped pursuing him
decisions.reason: "From after him" means from following him; the commanders broke off the chase, as their orders required (verse 31).

decisions.choice: realized
decisions.reason: Readable says "realized" for "saw", since they understood rather than looked.

source.text: וְאִ֗ישׁ מָשַׁ֤ךְ בַּקֶּ֨שֶׁת֙ לְתֻמּ֔וֹ וַיַּכֶּה֙ אֶת־מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בֵּ֥ין הַדְּבָקִ֖ים וּבֵ֣ין הַשִּׁרְיָ֑ן וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לְרַכָּב֗וֹ הֲפֹ֥ךְ יָדְךָ֛ וְהוֹצִיאֵ֥נִי מִן־הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֖ה כִּ֥י הָחֳלֵֽיתִי׃

records.literal_gloss: And a man drew on the bow in his innocence and struck [the] king of Israel between the scales and between the armor; and he said to his chariot driver, turn your hand and bring me out from the camp, for I am wounded.

en.L: And a man drew the bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the joints of the armor and the breastplate. And he said to his chariot driver, "Turn your hand and take me out of the camp, for I am wounded."
en.B: But a man drew his bow at random and hit the king of Israel between the joints of his scale armor and the breastplate. The king said to his chariot driver, "Turn around and get me out of the battle, because I am wounded."
en.R: But an Aramean soldier shot an arrow without aiming at anyone in particular. It hit the king of Israel where his armor joined together. The king said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and take me away from the fighting! I am wounded."

decisions.choice: in his innocence: at random, without aiming at the king
decisions.reason: The word means simplicity or innocence. The archer shot without a particular target and with no idea who he hit. What the Aramean commanders failed to do with their orders, one unaimed arrow did, as Micaiah had said.

decisions.choice: between the scales and the armor: at a gap where pieces of armor met
alternatives: between the joints and the coat of mail
between the lower armor and the breastplate
decisions.reason: The two words are rare and their exact meaning is not certain. The first, from a root meaning "to cling, to join", may name the joints or the small overlapping plates of scale armor; the second names a coat of mail or breastplate. The arrow struck at a weak point where they met, perhaps under the arm or at the waist.

decisions.choice: turn your hand: turn the chariot around
decisions.reason: The driver holds the reins in his hand; to turn his hand is to turn the horses.

decisions.choice: the camp: the army, the battle lines
decisions.reason: Here "camp" means the army drawn up in battle, so to be taken out of it is to leave the fighting.

decisions.choice: an Aramean soldier
decisions.reason: Readable says that the archer was one of the enemy, which the context makes plain.

decisions.choice: joints ... breastplate / where his armor joined together
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced name the two parts of the armor; Readable gives the sense that matters, a gap in the armor (m2).

source.text: וַתַּעֲלֶ֤ה הַמִּלְחָמָה֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא וְהַמֶּ֗לֶךְ הָיָ֧ה מָעֳמָ֛ד בַּמֶּרְכָּבָ֖ה נֹ֣כַח אֲרָ֑ם וַיָּ֣מָת בָּעֶ֔רֶב וַיִּ֥צֶק דַּֽם־הַמַּכָּ֖ה אֶל־חֵ֥יק הָרָֽכֶב׃

records.literal_gloss: And went up the battle on that day, and the king was propped up in the chariot opposite Aram; and he died in the evening, and poured out [the] blood of the wound into [the] bottom of the chariot.

en.L: And the battle went up on that day, and the king was propped up in the chariot facing Aram; and he died in the evening, and the blood of the wound poured out into the bottom of the chariot.
en.B: All that day the battle grew fiercer, and the king was held upright in his chariot facing the Arameans. He died at evening, and blood from the wound flowed down into the floor of the chariot.
en.R: The battle grew worse all that day. The king stayed propped up in his chariot, facing the Arameans. In the evening he died. The blood from his wound had run down onto the floor of the chariot.

decisions.choice: the battle went up: the battle rose, grew fierce
decisions.reason: The fighting increased in intensity through the day.

decisions.choice: propped up in the chariot facing Aram: kept upright so the troops would not lose heart
decisions.reason: Instead of leaving the field as he had ordered (verse 34), the king was held upright in his chariot, facing the enemy, perhaps so that his army would not see that he was wounded. He bled to death through the day.

decisions.choice: the blood of the wound: preparing for verse 38
decisions.reason: The detail of the blood in the chariot leads to verse 38, where the dogs lick up Ahab's blood as Yahweh had said (21:19).

decisions.choice: grew fierce / grew worse
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "went up" means here (m1).

source.text: וַיַּעֲבֹ֤ר הָרִנָּה֙ בַּֽמַּחֲנֶ֔ה כְּבֹ֥א הַשֶּׁ֖מֶשׁ לֵאמֹ֑ר אִ֥ישׁ אֶל־עִיר֖וֹ וְאִ֥ישׁ אֶל־אַרְצֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: And passed the cry through the camp at the going of the sun, saying, [each] man to his city, and [each] man to his land.

en.L: And the cry passed through the camp as the sun went down, saying, "Each man to his city, and each man to his land!"
en.B: As the sun was setting, a shout went through the army: "Every man to his town! Every man to his own land!"
en.R: As the sun went down, the order was shouted all through the army: "Everyone go home to your own town and your own land!"

decisions.choice: each man to his city: the army disbanded
decisions.reason: The call sends every soldier home: with the king dead, the campaign is over. It fulfills Micaiah's vision of the flock without a shepherd, each returning home in peace (verse 17).

decisions.choice: the cry: a ringing shout
decisions.reason: The word is used of a loud cry, of joy or of alarm. Here it is the order shouted through the ranks.

decisions.choice: the order was shouted
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the cry was an order to the troops (m2).

source.text: וַיָּ֣מָת הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיָּב֖וֹא שֹׁמְר֑וֹן וַיִּקְבְּר֥וּ אֶת־הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בְּשֹׁמְרֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: And died the king, and he came [to] Samaria, and they buried the king in Samaria.

en.L: And the king died, and he came [to] Samaria, and they buried the king in Samaria.
en.B: So the king died. He was brought to Samaria, and they buried him there.
en.R: So the king died. His body was brought back to Samaria, and he was buried there.

decisions.choice: he came to Samaria: his body was brought to Samaria
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says simply "he came". The dead king was carried back to his capital for burial. Some ancient translations read "they came".

decisions.choice: buried in Samaria: in the royal city his father built
decisions.reason: Omri, Ahab's father, had built Samaria and was buried there (16:24, 28).

decisions.choice: was brought / His body was brought
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "he came" means here (m1).

source.text: וַיִּשְׁטֹ֨ף אֶת־הָרֶ֜כֶב עַ֣ל׀בְּרֵכַ֣ת שֹׁמְר֗וֹן וַיָּלֹ֤קּוּ הַכְּלָבִים֙ אֶת־דָּמ֔וֹ וְהַזֹּנ֖וֹת רָחָ֑צוּ כִּדְבַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבֵּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And he washed the chariot by [the] pool of Samaria, and licked up the dogs his blood, and the prostitutes bathed, according to [the] word of Yahweh which he had spoken.

en.L: And one washed the chariot at the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked up his blood, and the prostitutes bathed, according to the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had spoken.
en.B: When they washed the chariot at the pool of Samaria, dogs licked up his blood, and the prostitutes bathed there, just as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had said.
en.R: Someone washed out the chariot at the pool in Samaria. Dogs licked up the king's blood, and prostitutes washed themselves in the pool. It happened just as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had said it would.

decisions.choice: the prostitutes bathed: prostitutes washed in the pool where his blood was washed out
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "and the prostitutes bathed". The point seems to be the shame of the king's end: his blood went to dogs and into water used by prostitutes. Some ancient readers took the words differently, as "they washed the armor" or "they washed his weapons", reading the word for prostitutes as a word for arms, but the Hebrew word is the ordinary word for prostitutes. Why the prostitutes are mentioned is not explained.

decisions.choice: according to the word of Yahweh: the fulfillment of 21:19
decisions.reason: After the murder of Naboth, Elijah told Ahab, "In the place where the dogs licked the blood of Naboth, the dogs will lick your blood, yes, yours" (21:19). Naboth was killed at Jezreel (21:1, 13), and Ahab's blood is licked up at Samaria. Because Ahab humbled himself, Yahweh delayed part of the judgment until his son's days (21:29); the rest is completed when Ahab's son Joram is killed and thrown on Naboth's land (2 Kings 9:25-26). The writer sees Ahab's death as the word of Yahweh coming true, as Micaiah also said (verses 17, 28).

decisions.choice: he washed: someone washed
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject; it means "the chariot was washed".

decisions.choice: the king's blood
decisions.reason: Readable names whose blood it was, since "his" could be read as the chariot driver's.

source.text: וְיֶתֶר֩ דִּבְרֵ֨י אַחְאָ֜ב וְכָל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֗ה וּבֵ֤ית הַשֵּׁן֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בָּנָ֔ה וְכָל־הֶעָרִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר בָּנָ֑ה הֲלֽוֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַיָּמִ֖ים לְמַלְכֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] rest of [the] matters of Ahab and all that he did, and [the] house of the ivory which he built, and all the cities which he built, are not they written on [the] book of [the] matters of the days of the kings of Israel?

en.L: And the rest of the matters of Ahab, and all that he did, and the house of ivory that he built, and all the cities that he built, are they not written in the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Israel?
en.B: The rest of the acts of Ahab, all that he did, the ivory palace he built and all the cities he built, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel.
en.R: Everything else Ahab did is written in the history of the kings of Israel. It tells about the palace he built and decorated with ivory, and all the cities he built.

decisions.choice: the house of ivory: a palace decorated with carved ivory
decisions.reason: The house was not made of ivory but adorned with ivory panels and inlays on its walls and furniture. Many carved ivory pieces have been found in the ruins of the royal buildings at Samaria. Amos later condemned the "houses of ivory" of Israel's rich (Amos 3:15; 6:4).

decisions.choice: the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Israel: a royal record now lost
decisions.reason: As at 14:19 and 16:5, the writer sends readers to a fuller record of the kings of Israel, which has not survived.

decisions.choice: are they not written ...?: a question that means "they are written"
decisions.reason: The standard closing formula for a reign in Kings.

decisions.choice: the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Israel / the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel / the history of the kings of Israel
decisions.reason: The source formula has one wording at each level throughout Kings. Balanced and Readable turn the question into a statement (m3).

decisions.choice: ivory palace / palace ... decorated with ivory
decisions.reason: "House" here is a royal palace; Readable says how the ivory was used (m1).

source.text: וַיִּשְׁכַּ֥ב אַחְאָ֖ב עִם־אֲבֹתָ֑יו וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אֲחַזְיָ֥הוּ בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו׃פ

records.literal_gloss: And lay down Ahab with his fathers, and reigned Ahaziah his son in his place.

en.L: And Ahab lay down with his fathers, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.
en.B: So Ahab rested with his ancestors, and his son Ahaziah became king in his place.
en.R: So Ahab died, and his son Ahaziah became king after him.

decisions.choice: lay down with his fathers: died
decisions.reason: This is the death formula of Kings (2:10; 16:6, 28). It is used here even though Ahab died in battle, so it does not mean a peaceful death; it says only that he joined his ancestors in death.

decisions.choice: Ahaziah: Ahab's son, king of Israel
decisions.reason: Not to be confused with Ahaziah son of Jehoram, a later king of Judah (2 Kings 8:24-26). His reign is introduced at verse 52.

decisions.choice: lay down with his fathers / rested with his ancestors / died
decisions.reason: The death formula is worded the same way at each level throughout Kings.

source.text: וִיהֽוֹשָׁפָט֙ בֶּן־אָסָ֔א מָלַ֖ךְ עַל־יְהוּדָ֑ה בִּשְׁנַ֣ת אַרְבַּ֔ע לְאַחְאָ֖ב מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king over Judah in [the] year four of Ahab king of Israel.

en.L: And Jehoshaphat son of Asa reigned over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.
en.B: In the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel, Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king over Judah.
en.R: Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king of Judah. It was the fourth year that Ahab had been king of Israel.

decisions.choice: the reign of Jehoshaphat: the account returns to Judah
decisions.reason: Kings now gives the formal account of Jehoshaphat's reign, which began years before the battle of this chapter (15:24). Further events of his reign are told in 2 Kings 3 and in 2 Chronicles 17-20.

decisions.choice: became king: began to reign
decisions.reason: With a date, the verb marks the start of the reign, as in the accession formula of 15:1, 9.

decisions.choice: the date first / two sentences
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the date first, as the accession formula does throughout Kings; Readable splits it into two sentences, as in 15:1.

source.text: יְהוֹשָׁפָ֗ט בֶּן־שְׁלֹשִׁ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ בְּמָלְכ֔וֹ וְעֶשְׂרִ֤ים וְחָמֵשׁ֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְשֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔וֹ עֲזוּבָ֖ה בַּת־שִׁלְחִֽי׃

records.literal_gloss: Jehoshaphat [was] a son of thirty and five year[s] when he became king, and twenty and five year[s] he reigned in Jerusalem; and [the] name of his mother [was] Azubah daughter of Shilhi.

en.L: Jehoshaphat [was] thirty-five years old when he became king, and twenty-five years he reigned in Jerusalem, and the name of his mother [was] Azubah daughter of Shilhi.
en.B: Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king. He reigned in Jerusalem twenty-five years, and his mother's name was Azubah daughter of Shilhi.
en.R: Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-five years. His mother was Azubah, the daughter of Shilhi.

decisions.choice: a son of thirty-five years: thirty-five years old
decisions.reason: Hebrew gives a person's age as being "a son of" so many years.

decisions.choice: the name of his mother: the queen mother
decisions.reason: For the kings of Judah, Kings names each king's mother (15:2, 10). The king's mother held an honored position at court (2:19; 15:13).

decisions.choice: thirty-five years old
decisions.reason: Every level gives the age in the normal English way (m1).

source.text: וַיֵּ֗לֶךְ בְּכָל־דֶּ֛רֶךְ אָסָ֥א אָבִ֖יו לֹא־סָ֣ר מִמֶּ֑נּוּ לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת הַיָּשָׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And he walked in all [the] way of Asa his father; not he turned aside from it, doing the right in [the] eyes of Yahweh.

en.L: And he walked in all the way of Asa his father; he did not turn aside from it, doing the right in [the] eyes of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: He followed all the ways of his father Asa and did not turn aside from them, doing what was right in the sight of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: He lived the way his father Asa had lived and never turned away from it. He did what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said was right.

decisions.choice: walked in the way of Asa: lived as Asa had lived
decisions.reason: To walk in someone's way is to follow his example. Asa had done what was right in Yahweh's eyes (15:11).

decisions.choice: doing the right in the eyes of Yahweh: the verdict on a good king
decisions.reason: This is the verdict formula of Kings for a king who served Yahweh (15:11).

decisions.choice: did the right in [the] eyes of / did what was right in the sight of / did what the LORD said was right
decisions.reason: The verdict formula has one wording at each level throughout these books.

source.text: אַ֥ךְ הַבָּמ֖וֹת לֹֽא־סָ֑רוּ ע֥וֹד הָעָ֛ם מְזַבְּחִ֥ים וּֽמְקַטְּרִ֖ים בַּבָּמֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: Only the high places were not removed; still the people [were] sacrificing and making smoke at the high places.

en.L: Only the high places were not removed; the people were still sacrificing and burning incense at the high places.
en.B: However, the high places were not removed; the people still offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places.
en.R: But the hilltop shrines were not removed. The people still offered sacrifices and burned incense at the hilltop shrines.

decisions.choice: verse numbers: Hebrew 22:44-54 is 22:43-53 in many Bibles
decisions.reason: This translation numbers verses as the Hebrew text does. Many Bibles print this verse as the second half of verse 43, and so number the rest of the chapter one lower: Hebrew 22:45-54 is 22:44-53 there. (A smaller difference comes at verse 21.) The words are the same; only the numbers differ.

decisions.choice: the high places: local places of worship
decisions.reason: High places were local shrines, often on hills, with an altar. Even when they were used to worship Yahweh, sacrifice there went against the law's demand to worship at the one place Yahweh chose (Deuteronomy 12:13-14). Asa did not remove them either (15:14).

decisions.choice: making smoke: burning offerings, or burning incense
decisions.reason: The verb means to make something go up in smoke. It can refer to burning incense or to burning parts of an offering. With "sacrificing" it describes the regular worship at the shrines.

decisions.choice: hilltop shrines
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced say "high places"; Readable says "hilltop shrines", as these books do throughout.

source.text: וַיַּשְׁלֵ֥ם יְהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט עִם־מֶ֥לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: And made peace Jehoshaphat with [the] king of Israel.

en.L: And Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel.
en.B: Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel.
en.R: Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel.

decisions.choice: made peace with the king of Israel: ended the long war between the kingdoms
decisions.reason: Judah and Israel had been at war since the kingdom divided (14:30; 15:6, 16). Jehoshaphat ended it and allied himself with the house of Ahab, as this chapter's campaign shows. His son Jehoram married Ahab's daughter (2 Kings 8:18).

decisions.choice: also
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "also" to link this note to the summary of the reign.

source.text: וְיֶ֨תֶר דִּבְרֵ֧י יְהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט וּגְבוּרָת֥וֹ אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂ֖ה וַאֲשֶׁ֣ר נִלְחָ֑ם הֲלֹֽא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַיָּמִ֖ים לְמַלְכֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] rest of [the] matters of Jehoshaphat and his might which he did and what he waged war, are not they written on [the] book of [the] matters of the days of the kings of Judah?

en.L: And the rest of the matters of Jehoshaphat, and his might that he showed, and how he made war, are they not written in the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Judah?
en.B: The rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, the might he showed and how he waged war, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah.
en.R: Everything else Jehoshaphat did is written in the history of the kings of Judah. It tells about his great deeds and the wars he fought.

decisions.choice: his might and how he made war: his military strength and campaigns
decisions.reason: "Might" is a king's strength and deeds of power, especially in war (16:5). Chronicles tells of Jehoshaphat's armies and his wars (2 Chronicles 17:12-19; 20:1-30).

decisions.choice: the book of the matters of the days of the kings of Judah: a royal record of Judah now lost
decisions.reason: As at 14:29 and 15:7, the writer sends readers to a fuller record of Judah's kings.

decisions.choice: the source formula
decisions.reason: As in verse 39, with Judah; Balanced and Readable state as a fact what the Hebrew asks as a question.

source.text: וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ הַקָּדֵ֔שׁ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִשְׁאַ֔ר בִּימֵ֖י אָסָ֣א אָבִ֑יו בִּעֵ֖ר מִן־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

records.literal_gloss: And [the] rest of the male cult prostitute[s] who remained in [the] days of Asa his father he purged from the land.

en.L: And the remnant of the male cult prostitutes who remained in the days of Asa his father, he purged from the land.
en.B: He also drove out of the land the rest of the male shrine prostitutes who were left from the days of his father Asa.
en.R: He also got rid of the rest of the men who served as prostitutes at the shrines. Some of them had stayed in the land even after his father Asa's time.

decisions.choice: the male shrine prostitutes: men who served at the shrines of other gods
decisions.reason: As at 14:24 and 15:12, the word means "consecrated ones" and names men attached to the shrines, whom the law forbids (Deuteronomy 23:18). Most understand them as men who offered sex as part of the worship there; the evidence for the sexual sense is not certain. Asa had driven them out (15:12), but some remained; Jehoshaphat finished the work.

decisions.choice: purged: removed completely
decisions.reason: The verb means to burn or sweep away, and is used of removing evil from the land (Deuteronomy 13:6).

decisions.choice: the men who served as prostitutes at the shrines
decisions.reason: Readable explains the term with a short description, as at 15:12 (m1).

source.text: וּמֶ֥לֶךְ אֵ֛ין בֶּאֱד֖וֹם נִצָּ֥ב מֶֽלֶךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: And king there was not in Edom; a deputy [was] king.

en.L: And [there was] no king in Edom; a deputy [was] king.
en.B: There was then no king in Edom; a deputy ruled as king.
en.R: At that time Edom had no king of its own. A governor ruled the country.

decisions.choice: no king in Edom: Edom was under Judah's control
decisions.reason: Edom lay south of the Dead Sea. A deputy, probably appointed by Judah, ruled in place of a king. This explains how Jehoshaphat could build ships at Ezion-geber, on the Red Sea coast in Edom's territory (verse 49; 9:26). Later Edom had its own king again (2 Kings 3:9; 8:20).

decisions.choice: deputy: an appointed officer
decisions.reason: The word is used for officers appointed over districts (4:5, 7). The short clause "a deputy king" may also mean "the deputy was king" or "a deputy acted as king".

decisions.choice: A governor ruled the country.
decisions.reason: Readable says "governor" for the appointed deputy (m2).

source.text: יְהוֹשָׁפָ֡ט עָשָׂה֩ אֳנִיּ֨וֹת תַּרְשִׁ֜ישׁ לָלֶ֧כֶת אוֹפִ֛ירָה לַזָּהָ֖ב וְלֹ֣א הָלָ֑ךְ כִּֽי־נִשְׁבְּר֥וּ אֳנִיּ֖וֹת בְּעֶצְי֥וֹן גָּֽבֶר׃

records.literal_gloss: Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for the gold, and not it went, for were broken [the] ships at Ezion-geber.

en.L: Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but it did not go, for the ships were broken at Ezion-geber.
en.B: Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to sail to Ophir for gold, but they never sailed, because the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber.
en.R: Jehoshaphat built large trading ships to sail to Ophir and bring back gold. But they never sailed, because the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber.

decisions.choice: made: the reading of the Hebrew tradition
alternatives: Jehoshaphat had ten ships of Tarshish
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text is written with consonants that would mean "ten", but the traditional reading, marked in the margin of the Hebrew text, is "made". This translation follows the traditional reading; with the written form the clause would say that Jehoshaphat had ten ships of Tarshish.

decisions.choice: ships of Tarshish: large ocean-going trading ships
decisions.reason: Tarshish was a distant port, probably in the far west of the Mediterranean. "Ships of Tarshish" came to mean large seagoing ships of the kind used on long trade voyages, whatever their route (10:22). These were built on the Red Sea.

decisions.choice: Ophir: a land famous for its gold
decisions.reason: Solomon's fleet sailed from Ezion-geber to Ophir and brought back gold (9:26-28; 10:11). Where Ophir was is not known; Arabia, East Africa and India have all been suggested.

decisions.choice: the ships were wrecked: told also in 2 Chronicles 20:35-37
decisions.reason: Chronicles says that Jehoshaphat built these ships in partnership with Ahaziah king of Israel, and that the prophet Eliezer foretold they would be wrecked because of that alliance. Kings says that Jehoshaphat refused Ahaziah's offer of sailors (verse 50); the two accounts may describe different stages of the venture.

decisions.choice: large trading ships
decisions.reason: Readable says what "ships of Tarshish" were (m2) instead of the name.

source.text: אָ֠ז אָמַ֞ר אֲחַזְיָ֤הוּ בֶן־אַחְאָב֙ אֶל־יְה֣וֹשָׁפָ֔ט יֵלְכ֧וּ עֲבָדַ֛י עִם־עֲבָדֶ֖יךָ בָּאֳנִיּ֑וֹת וְלֹ֥א אָבָ֖ה יְהוֹשָׁפָֽט׃

records.literal_gloss: Then said Ahaziah son of Ahab to Jehoshaphat, let go my servants with your servants in the ships; and not was willing Jehoshaphat.
